action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left temporal-parietal 4.9 cm mass with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, extensive vasogenic edema involving the optic radiation and 5 mm rightward midline shift
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol: DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the left temporal-parietal mass and its mass effect and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with a standardised tumour protocol characterises the lesion and its mass effect, identifies the target for tissue sampling and is required before surgery (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio 4.6 in the enhancing rim, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and identifying the target for tissue sampling
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion) to assess tumor vascularity and target the highest-grade region for tissue sampling
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and points to the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA ratio 9.3 with prominent lipid and lactate peaks in the enhancing component, supporting a high-grade neoplasm
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterize the tumor metabolic profile
action_criteria.rationale: A raised Cho/NAA ratio with lipid and lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not replace tissue (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial primary malignancy or metastatic disease
action_criteria.label: Order contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis if a solitary metastasis remains on the differential
action_criteria.rationale: A single necrotic mass at 71 can be a metastasis; body staging is optional when the imaging favours a primary glioma.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindication to surgery: normal blood count, platelets and coagulation, eGFR 64 with BUN 22; type and screen completed; ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP raised
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory work-up: CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) and type and screen before neurosurgery
action_criteria.rationale: Platelets, coagulation and a type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure, with baseline renal function, glucose and potassium before dexamethasone.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: KPS 70, ECOG 2: independent in self-care but no longer driving or managing her household
action_criteria.label: Record performance status (Karnofsky and ECOG) at this visit
action_criteria.rationale: At 71, performance status selects between treatment regimens after the integrated diagnosis; KPS below 70 is the unfavourable threshold (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Language left-lateralised; Wernicke area activation 6 mm and angular gyrus activation 3 mm from the enhancing margin
action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI for language lateralisation and mapping of Wernicke area and the angular gyrus before surgery
action_criteria.rationale: A dominant temporoparietal tumour centred in the superior temporal and angular gyri in a patient with anomia; functional MRI shows how close language cortex lies before resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left arcuate fasciculus displaced 4 mm from the margin; optic radiation within the FLAIR abnormality 2 mm from the margin
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the left arcuate fasciculus and optic radiation before surgery
action_criteria.rationale: The FLAIR abnormality involves the optic radiation and the arcuate fasciculus runs along the superior margin; tractography defines the subcortical limit of resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H IHC negative, ATRX retained and MGMT promoter methylated, with TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification and +7/-10
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left temporoparietal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: QT risk from hydroxychloroquine, increased by steroid hypokalaemia and by ondansetron; antacid spacing for hydroxychloroquine; co-trimoxazole excluded by the sulfonamide allergy
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of dexamethasone, and of the later chemoradiation supportive drugs, with her hydroxychloroquine, losartan and calcium carbonate, and her sulfonamide allergy
action_criteria.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine prolongs the QT interval, and dexamethasone and the antiemetics used with temozolomide can add to that risk; the sulfonamide allergy changes Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: 5 mm midline shift and mass effect create a risk of herniation
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiotherapy, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis: the patient has a documented sulfonamide allergy
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a specific thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and associated bleeding risk
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left temporoparietal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping (awake language mapping only if her naming and comprehension allow the intraoperative tasks, otherwise asleep resection with subcortical monitoring), with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 71 with KPS 70 and a methylated MGMT promoter, hypofractionated radiotherapy 40 Gy in 15 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Perry 2017; EANO 2021), or temozolomide alone if radiotherapy is not feasible.
Obtain a baseline ECG (QTc) and monitor potassium on dexamethasone, given the QT-prolonging effect of hydroxychloroquine, and avoid adding other QT-prolonging drugs such as ondansetron where possible
Prescribe Pneumocystis prophylaxis with dapsone, atovaquone or inhaled pentamidine during chemoradiation, avoiding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole because of the sulfonamide allergy

differential.key_features: A single ring-enhancing mass at 71 can be a solitary metastasis; never smoker, staging CT negative, infiltrative edema along white matter tracts favours a primary glioma, and tissue is glial
Immunocompetent; ring enhancement with central necrosis is atypical for PCNSL, which usually shows homogeneous enhancement with central DWI restriction; tissue shows a GFAP-positive glioma

Elevated ESR/CRP/RF in context of RA may suggest neurological RA manifestation; however, a large focal necrotic ring-enhancing mass without leptomeningeal enhancement is not consistent with vasculitis or rheumatoid meningitis, and tissue shows glioblastoma
No fever, no leukocytosis; restricted diffusion is at the enhancing rim (not centrally, as in pyogenic pus); elevated rCBV is inconsistent with abscess, and tissue shows a glioma
No prior demyelinating history; thick closed ring enhancement, central necrosis, and markedly elevated rCBV are atypical for tumefactive MS which usually shows open-ring enhancement

key_clinical_evidence: Six weeks of progressive anomia, episodic memory impairment and a right homonymous hemianopia with morning headaches in a 71-year-old woman localise to the left temporoparietal region and require urgent contrast-enhanced MRI before the symptoms are attributed to rheumatoid CNS disease

The left temporal-parietal MRI mass with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, extensive perilesional FLAIR hyperintensity, and 5 mm midline shift is imaging-characteristic of a high-grade primary brain neoplasm

Elevated ESR, CRP, RF, and anti-CCP antibodies are chronic features of the patient's known seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and do not indicate neurological RA or CNS vasculitis; the imaging findings are not consistent with either diagnosis
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV 4.6) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/NAA 9.3, lipid-lactate peaks) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help target biopsy to the highest-grade region

The tumour lies in dominant language cortex: functional MRI places Wernicke area 6 mm and the angular gyrus 3 mm from the margin, and DTI shows the optic radiation within the FLAIR abnormality; these plan the extent of a maximal safe resection

Tissue establishes glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 (IDH1 R132H negative, ATRX retained, MGMT methylated, TERT mutation, EGFR amplification, +7/-10); imaging alone cannot substitute for the integrated diagnosis
Over 70 with KPS 70 and a methylated MGMT promoter, hypofractionated radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 fractions) with temozolomide is the standard (Perry 2017; EANO 2021)

Hydroxychloroquine prolongs the QT interval, so dexamethasone hypokalaemia and QT-prolonging antiemetics need an ECG and potassium check, and the sulfonamide allergy rules out co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis
She has had no seizure, so no prophylactic antiseizure medication is started (AIOM); lumbar puncture is contraindicated by the 5 mm midline shift

metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from Stoyanov et al. (Cureus, 2022) 'The Rapid Development of Glioblastoma: A Report of Two Cases' (PMID 35911333, PMC9314278, CC-BY 4.0). Case 2 in that report is a 74-year-old female with rapidly progressive IDH-wildtype WHO grade 4 GBM confirmed histologically (microvascular proliferation, necrosis) with TERT promoter mutation and EGFR amplification. The present case uses that confirmed GBM as clinical seed: adapted to a 71-year-old Korean-American female with left temporal-parietal location, anomia/memory/right hemianopia presentation, and an RA-driven inflammatory red herring; demographics, tumor location, molecular detail, and clinical narrative are original.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Soon-Yi Park is a 71-year-old right-handed retired Korean-American elementary school teacher with a background history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), hypertension, and osteoporosis who is admitted to the neurology service for evaluation of subacute progressive cognitive decline and a right visual field deficit discovered by her ophthalmologist. Her symptoms began approximately six weeks ago, when her husband noticed that she was struggling to find words during conversation, mispronouncing familiar names and substituting incorrect words, which she had never done before. Over the ensuing weeks, she became increasingly forgetful, repeating questions she had just asked and forgetting appointments. She lost her way driving home from a grocery store she had frequented for over 15 years. Her ophthalmologist, whom she visited two weeks ago for her routine annual check, identified a right homonymous visual field defect on automated perimetry and referred her urgently to neurology. Her husband also reports that she has developed progressively worsening headaches over the past five weeks, predominantly left-sided and worse in the morning upon waking, occasionally accompanied by nausea. She has not vomited. There has been no seizure activity witnessed by the family. Her rheumatologist was consulted by telephone approximately three weeks ago and initially attributed the cognitive symptoms to possible rheumatoid CNS involvement (rheumatoid meningitis or vasculitis), given elevated inflammatory markers on her most recent laboratory work, and increased her hydroxychloroquine to 200 mg twice daily; however, her symptoms continued to worsen despite this adjustment. She denies any new joint flares, skin rash, oral ulcers, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She has not had recent travel or sick contacts. She was brought to the emergency department today after her husband found her unable to recognize her daughter's photograph during a family video call.

Follows two-step commands reliably but fails a three-step command. Short-term memory markedly impaired: recalls 0 out of 3 objects at five minutes.
